questions.question: Before a host ever sends a tools/call, what exactly does the model see about a tool?
options: The tool's full server side implementation, its source code, and stored secrets
The complete registry server.json entry the tool was originally published under
The tool's name, description, input schema, and any annotations the server sent
A cached session identifier the server assigned during an earlier handshake
questions.explanation: The model only sees the definition fields from tools/list, name, description, inputSchema, and annotations when the server sent them, never the server's implementation, a registry entry, or a session, since 2026-07-28 has none of those.

questions.question: A drafted close_ticket call targets a tool with no annotations block at all. What must the host do before the client sends anything?
options: Wait for a list_changed notification before deciding whether to confirm
Send the call immediately, since a missing annotations block means the tool is safe
Reject the call outright, since a tool with no annotations is invalid
Treat the tool as destructive by default and confirm with a human first
questions.explanation: readOnlyHint defaults to false and destructiveHint defaults to true, so a tool shipped with no annotations block at all is destructive under the specification's own defaults, and the host should confirm with a human before sending it.

questions.question: A tools/call result comes back with isError true because a required argument was missing. What should the model do next?
options: Read the explanation in content and retry with corrected arguments and a new id
Resend the identical call again, because most transient failures resolve themselves
Wait for the server to send an input_required result before trying again
Stop the whole conversation, since isError true always means the call cannot be retried
questions.explanation: A tool execution error is a normal result with isError true and actionable content the model can read, and it retries with corrected arguments using a fresh id, which is a different mechanism from the input_required pattern.

questions.question: An open_ticket call comes back with resultType input_required. How must the client's retry differ from the original request?
options: It omits requestState entirely, since the server already has that context
It uses a new JSON-RPC id and echoes requestState back exactly
It reuses the same JSON-RPC id so the server can match the two calls
It sends the request over a newly opened subscriptions/listen stream instead
questions.explanation: An MRTR retry must use a new JSON-RPC id and echo requestState byte for byte when the server sent one, so reusing the original id or inventing a different state value breaks the pattern the specification defines.

questions.question: The model tries a tool name the server does not expose and gets back a JSON-RPC error coded -32602. What should the loop do next?
options: Convert the error into an isError true result and retry with corrections
Open an input_required round trip to ask the user which tool to use
Move on without resending the identical call, since nothing about the request changed
Resend the exact same tools/call again with the same arguments
questions.explanation: A protocol error such as an unknown tool gives the model nothing to fix, so a well built loop does not retry the identical request, unlike a tool execution error, which does invite a corrected retry with a new id.

questions.question: Why does returning tools/list in the same deterministic order every turn matter for a host holding a long conversation?
options: It allows the host to skip sending required protocol metadata on later requests
It is required before the client can open a subscriptions/listen stream at all
It lets the server skip validating arguments on every later call it receives
It keeps the cached prefix stable and protects the provider's own prompt cache
questions.explanation: Most model providers cache the prompt prefix that holds the tool array, so a stable and deterministic order lets the host reuse that context across turns without invalidating the provider's cache and paying for the definitions again.
